Prevention: Clear weeds which serve as alternative hosts for the pest.
Plough and harrow the field after harvest to cover looper infested plant remains with soil.
Use looper tolerant varieties such as “Savoy
Practise crop rotation with non-brassicas for at least two consecutive growing seasons to prevent multiplication of the cabbage looper.
Brassicas, beets, cotton, potato, legumes (such as alfalfa, cowpea, peanuts and soybeans), because they are also hosts of this pest.
Monitoring: Monitor the adult moth occurrence with traps: hang plastic bottles on sticks in the field, bottles are less than a ¼ filled with fermented fruit juice or local brews to attract the moths.
If you find 1 to 2 looper moths in a bottle per day then it alerts you that larval damage will soon occur.
Once moths were found, Inspect plants regularly (at least once per week) for the presence of actively moving 2 to 4 cm green caterpillars, and for small to big feeding windows on leaves.
Check more often (twice a week) if population increases.
Larvae are of green colour with four thin white stripes and arch the body as it moves.; Search for larvae and looper pupae underside of the leaves
Consider control measures once 2-4 small sized caterpillars (< 2 cm) are found per plant.
Should you find many caterpillars that are bigger than 3 to 4 cm caterpillars and pupae, you might be too late.
Direct Control: Hand picking and mechanical destruction of the caterpillars if few
Apply neem solutions, made of 50g of ripen neem seed powder mixed with 15 litres of water
Remove and destroy the crop debris after harvesting because loopers live in there.
Restrictions: When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label.
